sections.title: Active and passive forms: one verb, two sets of endings

body.p: Many verbs come in pairs: an active form and a passive-form partner.

ex.en: I'm washing the car. / I'm washing (myself).
I'm dressing the child. / I'm getting dressed.

ex.el: Έχασα το πορτοφόλι μου. / Χάθηκα στην Πλάκα.
ex.en: I lost my wallet. / I got lost in Plaka.

body.p: Many very common verbs have **only passive forms** and active meaning (called **αποθετικά**, deponents): **έρχομαι** come, **κάθομαι** sit, **σκέφτομαι** think, **χρειάζομαι** need, **αισθάνομαι** feel, **εργάζομαι** work, **θυμάμαι** remember, **κοιμάμαι** sleep, **φοβάμαι** fear, **γίνομαι** become, **δέχομαι** accept, **εύχομαι** wish, **μάχομαι** fight, **ονειρεύομαι** dream, **ντρέπομαι** be ashamed, **αρνούμαι** refuse, **αναρωτιέμαι** wonder.
Note that deponents can have a **direct object** in the accusative (**χρειάζομαι βοήθεια, σε σκέφτομαι**), unlike true passives.

check.why: The passive form here is reflexive: I dress myself.

check.q: Which verb has no active form?
check.why: Έρχομαι is deponent: only passive endings, active meaning.

body.p: A **transitive** verb takes a direct object (accusative): **βλέπω τη θάλασσα, τρώω ψωμί**. An **intransitive** verb does not: **κοιμάμαι, έρχομαι, πεθαίνω**.
Many Greek verbs are **both**, with the same form (like English "open, break, change"):

head: Transitive
Intransitive
rows: Άνοιξε την πόρτα. He opened the door.
Η πόρτα άνοιξε. The door opened.
Άλλαξα γνώμη. I changed my mind.
Ο καιρός άλλαξε. The weather changed.
Σταμάτησε το αυτοκίνητο. She stopped the car.
Το αυτοκίνητο σταμάτησε. The car stopped.
Γύρισε το κλειδί. Turn the key.
Αύξησαν τις τιμές. They raised prices.
Οι τιμές αυξήθηκαν. Prices rose. (passive form)
Το νερό βράζει. The water is boiling.

body.p: Other verbs use the **passive form for the intransitive**: **σπάω το ποτήρι / το ποτήρι έσπασε** (same form) but **καίω το χαρτί / καίγομαι** (I'm burning, I burn myself); **ζεσταίνω το φαγητό / ζεσταίνομαι** (I'm hot); **κλείνω την πόρτα / κλείνομαι** (I shut myself in) but **το μαγαζί κλείνει** (the shop closes).

check.why: Σπάω is intransitive too, in the active: έσπασε. (Σπάστηκε is rare.)
Κρυώνω is intransitive in the active: "I'm cold". (Κάνει κρύο means "the weather is cold".)

body.p: **Direct object: accusative.** **Βλέπω τον Γιάννη. Αγόρασα ένα βιβλίο.**
**Indirect object (the receiver): σε + accusative, or the genitive of a weak pronoun.**

ex.en: I gave the book to Maria.

ex.el: Είπα στον πατέρα μου την αλήθεια.
ex.en: I told my father the truth.

body.p: Verbs of giving and communicating take both objects: **δίνω, στέλνω, δείχνω, λέω, εξηγώ, φέρνω, δανείζω, προσφέρω, χαρίζω, γράφω, τηλεφωνώ** (only indirect: **τηλεφωνώ στη μητέρα μου / της τηλεφωνώ**), **απαντώ** (**απάντησε στο email / μου απάντησε**).

**Verbs with an indirect object only** (English direct object!): **αρέσω** "please", **τηλεφωνώ** "phone", **μοιάζω** "resemble" (**μοιάζει της μητέρας του** or **μοιάζει με τη μητέρα του**), **χρωστάω** "owe" (**σου χρωστάω**), **ανήκω** "belong" (**σε ποιον ανήκει;**), **επιτρέπω** "allow" (**μου επιτρέπει να...**).

ex.en: I like olives. (literally: olives please me)

body.p: **Αρέσω** works backwards from English: the thing liked is the **subject** (and controls the verb ending), the person is the **genitive**: **Μου αρέσει το κρασί** "I like wine"; **Μου αρέσουν τα κρασιά** "I like the wines"; **Σου αρέσω;** "Do you like me?" (literally: do I please you?).

check.why: The thing liked is the subject: plural τα νησιά → αρέσουν.
Τηλεφωνώ takes σε + accusative (or a genitive pronoun: τηλεφώνησέ της).

body.p: Impersonal verbs have no personal subject and are used in the 3rd person singular.

**Weather:** **βρέχει** it's raining, **χιονίζει** it's snowing, **φυσάει** it's windy, **αστράφτει** there's lightning, **βροντάει** it's thundering, **ξημερώνει** day is breaking, **νυχτώνει** night is falling, **κάνει κρύο / ζέστη / καλό καιρό** it's cold / hot / nice weather.

**Necessity and possibility:** **πρέπει** must, **χρειάζεται** is necessary, **μπορεί** may, might, **γίνεται** is possible, can be done, **επιτρέπεται / απαγορεύεται** is allowed / forbidden, **αξίζει** is worth it, **συμφέρει** pays, is worth it, **φτάνει** it's enough, **αρκεί** it suffices.

**Feeling and happening:** **μου αρέσει** I like, **με νοιάζει** I care, **με πειράζει** it bothers me, **μου λείπει** I miss, **μου φαίνεται** it seems to me, **συμβαίνει** it happens, **τυχαίνει** it happens (by chance), **πρόκειται για** it's about, **λέγεται ότι** it is said.

ex.el: Σε πειράζει αν ανοίξω το παράθυρο;
ex.en: Do you mind if I open the window?
I miss you. (literally: you are missing to me)

body.tip: **Πρέπει** never changes for person: **πρέπει να πάω, πρέπει να πας, πρέπει να πάμε**. The past is **έπρεπε**. Similarly **μπορεί να** "may (possibly)" stays 3rd singular, unlike **μπορώ** "I can".

body.p: **Μου λείπεις** "I miss you" works like αρέσω: the person missed is the subject. **Μου λείπουν οι φίλοι μου** "I miss my friends".

check.why: Πρέπει is impersonal; the person goes on the second verb.
The missed persons are the subject (λείπετε); the one who misses is the genitive (μου).

sections.title: Modal verbs: μπορώ, πρέπει, θέλω, ξέρω

body.p: The modals take **να + subjunctive** and carry the shades of ability, obligation, will and probability.
**Past and perfect of modals** distinguish "had to (and did)" from "should have":

ex.en: I had to leave early. (or: I should have left early)

body.p: **Probability scale**: **σίγουρα** certainly → **πρέπει να** must → **θα** will (probably) → **μάλλον** probably → **μπορεί να / ίσως** maybe → **δύσκολα** hardly.

check.why: Possibility is the impersonal μπορεί να. (Πρέπει να έχεις δίκιο means "you must be right".)
Absence of necessity in the past: δεν χρειαζόταν να.

sections.title: The passive voice proper: από, and when Greek avoids it

body.p: A true passive turns the object into the subject. The agent, if mentioned, takes **από** + accusative.

ex.el: Το βιβλίο γράφτηκε από τον Καζαντζάκη.
ex.en: The book was written by Kazantzakis.

ex.el: Ο κλέφτης συνελήφθη από την αστυνομία.
ex.en: The thief was arrested by the police.

body.p: Greek uses the passive **less** than English in speech, especially with an agent. Alternatives:

list: **Active with fronted object** (and doubling): **Το βιβλίο το έγραψε ο Καζαντζάκης** "The book was written by Kazantzakis".
**3rd person plural with no subject** ("they"): **Τον απέλυσαν** "He was fired"; **Μου έκλεψαν το ποδήλατο** "My bike was stolen".
**Impersonal passive** without agent in formal style: **Ανακοινώθηκε ότι...** "It was announced that...".

body.p: **Passives that do not exist.** Verbs with a genitive or σε-object (**τηλεφωνώ, αρέσω, μοιάζω**) cannot be made passive. Verbs of perception and thought often have only a limited passive.

check.why: Speech prefers the 3rd plural active with no subject.

check.q: "The museum was founded by the state":
options: Το μουσείο ιδρύθηκε με το κράτος.
Το μουσείο ιδρύθηκε από το κράτος.
check.answer: Το μουσείο ιδρύθηκε από το κράτος.
check.why: The agent of a passive takes από.

sections.title: Reflexive and reciprocal meanings of the passive form

body.p: The passive form often means "to/for oneself" (reflexive) or "each other" (reciprocal):

ex.en: See you tomorrow! (literally: we see each other tomorrow)
They haven't been on speaking terms for years.

body.p: The prefix **αυτο-** makes reflexive compounds in formal style: **αυτοκτονώ** commit suicide, **αυτοπροσδιορίζομαι** define oneself, **αυτοαναιρούμαι** contradict oneself. The prefix **αλληλο-** makes reciprocal ones: **αλληλοβοηθιόμαστε** we help each other, **αλληλοσυγχαίρονται** they congratulate each other.

check.why: Reciprocal passive: βλεπόμαστε.

sections.el: Ρήματα με δύο αντικείμενα και κατηγορούμενο
sections.title: Double objects and object complements

body.p: **Two accusatives** with verbs of teaching, asking, and some others: **Τον ρώτησα κάτι** "I asked him something", **Μας διδάσκει ιστορία** "(S)he teaches us history" (also **μας** as genitive), **Τον κέρασα έναν καφέ** "I treated him to a coffee", **Με λένε Μαρία** "They call me Maria".
**Object + predicate (object complement)**: verbs of naming, choosing, considering, making put a second noun or adjective after the object, agreeing with it:
In the passive, both become nominative: **Εξελέγη πρόεδρος** "He was elected president"; **Θεωρείται ο καλύτερος** "He is considered the best".

**Genitive objects** survive in a few formal phrases: **επωφελούμαι της ευκαιρίας** "take advantage of the opportunity" (everyday **επωφελούμαι από**), **μετέχω της εξουσίας** "share in power" (everyday **συμμετέχω σε**). Everyday Greek uses a preposition instead.

check.why: Object + bare predicate noun, both accusative: τη ... διευθύντρια.

body.p: Many verbs need a particular preposition. Learn them as chunks.

head: Verb + preposition
Meaning
Example
rows: Φροντίζει τη μητέρα της. Φρόντισε για τα εισιτήρια.
Η λέξη προέρχεται από τα αρχαία.

check.why: Εξαρτώμαι από.
Ενδιαφέρομαι για.

body.p: Greek makes verbs from nouns and adjectives with a small set of suffixes. Knowing them lets you understand, and often guess, new verbs.
**-άρω** is the everyday suffix for loans: **παρκάρω, φλερτάρω, σερβίρω** (-ίρω), **τσεκάρω, γκουγκλάρω, σκανάρω**. These verbs often have colloquial passives in **-άρομαι / -ιέμαι**.

**Prefixes** (see the prepositions document for meanings): **ξανα-** again (**ξαναρχίζω**), **ξε-** undo, out (**ξεκλειδώνω** unlock, **ξεφεύγω** escape), **παρα-** too much (**παρατρώω** overeat), **κατα-** completely, down (**καταστρέφω** destroy), **συν-** together (**συνεργάζομαι** cooperate), **προ-** before (**προβλέπω** foresee), **επανα-** re- (formal: **επαναλαμβάνω** repeat), **υπερ-** over (**υπερβάλλω** exaggerate), **υπο-** under (**υποτιμώ** underestimate).

ex.el: Η κυβέρνηση θέλει να απλοποιήσει τη διαδικασία.
ex.en: The government wants to simplify the procedure.
(S)he parked in front of the house.

check.why: Ξε- reverses: ξεκλειδώνω "unlock".
-ποιώ "make": απλοποιώ. (Απλώνω means "spread out".)

sections.title: Voice and meaning: pairs to master

body.p: Advanced Greek exploits the active/passive pair for nuance. Some pairs where the meaning shifts:

head: Active
Passive form
rows: πιάνομαι hold on to; get stiff; get caught
περνιέμαι be mistaken for; think too much of oneself

ex.en: I lost track of time and was late.
(S)he let herself go to the music.

body.p: **Middle voice and causation.** Some passive-form verbs mean "have something done to oneself": **κουρεύομαι** "get a haircut", **εξετάζομαι** "get examined (by a doctor)", **εμβολιάζομαι** "get vaccinated", **φωτογραφίζομαι** "have one's photo taken".

ex.en: I need to get a haircut.

check.why: Ξεχνιέμαι: get carried away, lose track of time.
The passive form κουρεύομαι means "have one's hair cut".

body.p: Formal Greek has learned synonyms for everyday verbs. Recognising pairs helps you read the press and adjust register in writing.

ex.en: Decisions were taken. (learned passive past of λαμβάνω)

body.p: **Learned passive pasts** in **-θην / -θη** forms appear in news and law: **ελήφθη** "was taken", **ετέθη** "was set", **εξελέγη** "was elected", **συνελήφθη** "was arrested", **απεβίωσε** "passed away", **διεξήχθη** "was conducted", **ανεστάλη** "was suspended", **εγκρίθηκε** "was approved" (regular).

ex.en: The flight was suspended due to bad weather.

check.q: The learned news form of "(he) was arrested":
check.why: Συνελήφθη is the learned passive past; the everyday equivalent is συλλήφθηκε. (Συνέλαβε is active "arrested".)
Παρέχω "provide".

el: Το ρήμα Γ΄: φωνή και σύνταξη
title: The verb III: voice, objects and verb types
blurb: Active and passive, reflexive and deponent verbs, transitivity, objects and cases, impersonal and modal verbs, and how verbs are built.

intro.p: The third verb document looks at the verb's relationships: **voice** (who does what to whom), **valency** (what objects and complements a verb needs, and in which case), and **verb types** (impersonal, modal, deponent). It ends with how Greek builds new verbs from nouns, adjectives and prefixes.

The central idea: Greek verbs have two sets of endings, **active** (-ω) and **passive** or **mediopassive** (-ομαι). The passive set does far more than make passives. It also marks reflexive actions (ντύνομαι "I get dressed"), reciprocal actions (αγαπιόμαστε "we love each other"), changes of state (ζεσταίνομαι "I get warm") and many verbs that simply exist only in that form (έρχομαι "I come").
